oewn-07521808-n.learner: a painful feeling that comes from knowing you have fallen short or done wrong
examples: Elizabeth tried to be diverted by them; but all sense of pleasure was lost in shame.
She was overpowered by shame and vexation.

oewn-07319716-n.learner: something that has turned out badly
examples: I shall tell Colonel Forster it will be quite a shame if he does not.

connotation.why: names the speaker's regret at the thing rather than a fact about it

oewn-14463603-n.learner: the condition of having lost your good name and other people's respect
examples: Her whole family lived in shame after the trial.

connotation.why: marks someone as fallen in other people's regard

oewn-04854529-n.learner: the quality of doing what is right and keeping away from what is wrong
examples: It has connected him nearer with virtue than any other feeling.

connotation.why: crediting someone with it approves of them rather than describes them

oewn-04856990-n.learner: right conduct in matters of sex
examples: a sister's sense of decency and virtue in such a point should admit of doubt
how little of permanent happiness could belong to a couple who were only brought together because their passions were stronger than their virtue

connotation.why: an approving and indirect name for chastity rather than a plain one

oewn-04854713-n.learner: one particular good quality of character
examples: His countenance, voice, and manner, had established him at once in the possession of every virtue.

connotation.why: names the quality as an excellence, so it praises whoever holds it

oewn-06743529-n.learner: a statement that someone has done something wrong
examples: There is, perhaps, a very faint shade of colour for the charge; but it seems to me very faint indeed.
The extravagance and general profligacy which he scrupled not to lay to Mr. Wickham's charge exceedingly shocked her

oewn-00831039-n.learner: looking after someone or something and being responsible for keeping them safe
examples: I always thought they were very unfit to have the charge of her

oewn-09929218-n.learner: a person who has been placed in your care
examples: Does your charge give you much trouble?

oewn-14009857-n.learner: a state in which a very strong feeling carries you away
examples: he left the room, fatigued with the raptures of his wife
I am quite in raptures with her beautiful little design for a table

oewn-14011586-n.learner: a state of very great happiness
examples: The rapture of Lydia on this occasion, her adoration of Mrs. Forster, the delight of Mrs. Bennet

oewn-01802947-v.learner: to fail to be or do what someone hoped for or expected
examples: Here are officers enough at Meryton to disappoint all the young ladies in the country.
Miss Bingley, however, was incapable of disappointing Mr. Darcy in anything

oewn-05201419-n.learner: the power to affect people or events, especially power that comes from your standing with others
examples: There could not exist in the world two men over whom Mr. Darcy could have such boundless influence.

oewn-11434722-n.learner: the effect that one thing or person has on another
examples: You appear to me, Mr. Darcy, to allow nothing for the influence of friendship and affection.

oewn-10481313-n.learner: someone who has the power to affect another person
examples: His older brother was a good influence on him.

oewn-10011405-n.learner: a person who is loved more than others
examples: the godson, the friend, the favourite of his father!
a great favourite with her Longbourn nieces

oewn-05798763-n.learner: a thing that someone likes better than others
examples: Of all the songs on the record, this one is my favourite.

oewn-10133522-n.learner: the one in a contest that people expect to win
examples: She started the final race as the clear favourite.

oewn-02211988-v.learner: to get something by paying money for it
examples: Look here, I have bought this bonnet.
you are always buying books

oewn-00685589-v.learner: to accept that something is true
examples: He says the delay was the weather's fault, but I don't buy that.

connotation.why: chosen over 'believe' it casts the claim as something being sold

oewn-02288941-v.learner: to pay someone illegally so that they will help you or do what you want
examples: They said the inspector had been bought and would report whatever he was told.

connotation.why: treats a person as something that can be purchased

oewn-04819517-n.learner: a polished quality of being graceful and having good taste
examples: Lady Catherine is far from requiring that elegance of dress in us which becomes herself and daughter.
I never saw such capacity, and taste, and application, and elegance, as you describe, united.

connotation.why: calling something elegance approves of its taste rather than reporting it

oewn-04819885-n.learner: the quality of a way of solving a problem that is neat and cleverly simple
examples: The elegance of her proof lay in its three short lines.

connotation.why: calling a solution elegant praises it rather than describing its shape

oewn-00902346-v.learner: to greet someone in a friendly way when they arrive
examples: Mrs. Collins welcomed her friend with the liveliest pleasure
They were not welcomed home very cordially by their mother.

oewn-02241988-v.learner: to be glad to accept something
examples: The board would welcome any suggestion that saves time.

oewn-01472727-v.learner: to take someone in, for example into your house
examples: They welcomed the stranger into their home and gave him a bed for the night.
